title: Antepartum haemorrhage
blurb: Tell placenta praevia from placental abruption, avoid a dangerous vaginal examination, give anti-D correctly and act first for the mother using RCOG GTG 63.
question: Mia, 32 weeks pregnant, phones the midwife-led unit with painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Her 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta. What should the midwife advise and avoid?

teach.body: Formally (RCOG GTG 63): antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from or into the genital tract, occurring from 24+0 weeks of pregnancy and before the birth of the baby. In plain English: any bleeding in the second half of pregnancy, including bleeding that stays hidden behind the placenta. The main causes are placenta praevia, placental abruption and local causes in the vulva, vagina or cervix; sometimes no cause is found ('unexplained APH').

head: Category
Blood loss
rows: Staining or streaking on underwear or pad
Less than 50 mL that has settled
50 to 1000 mL, no signs of shock
Over 1000 mL and/or signs of clinical shock
teach.caption: Visible loss often underestimates the total: a concealed abruption can bleed heavily behind the placenta. Look for shock and fetal compromise.

rows.label: Clues
values: Low placenta on scan, high presenting part

teach.caption: GTG 63 sections 4 and 7. Abruption is a clinical diagnosis: ultrasound misses about three-quarters of cases.

teach.h: No digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded
teach.body: If placenta praevia is possible (a previous scan showed a low placenta, the presenting part is high, or the bleed was painless), do not perform a digital vaginal examination until ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia. A finger through the cervix could provoke torrential bleeding. A speculum examination can help to see the cervix or a local cause.

items: Mia, 32 weeks, has painless bright red bleeding and a known low-lying placenta: placenta praevia is likely.
The midwife advises her to come straight into the obstetric unit by ambulance, as the MLU has no blood bank or theatre.
On arrival: pulse, BP, abdominal palpation (soft, non-tender) and fetal heart; no digital vaginal examination.
Mia is RhD-negative and not sensitised, so she will need anti-D and a Kleihauer test even though she had RAADP.
With bleeding heavier than spotting, she stays in hospital at least until it stops; steroids are considered.

teach.text: Painless bleeding does not mean 'nothing serious': placenta praevia can cause massive haemorrhage. And painful bleeding with little visible loss can be a large concealed abruption. Judge by her pulse, BP and the baby, not just the pad.

items: APH is bleeding from or into the genital tract from 24+0 weeks and before the birth.
Praevia: painless, soft uterus. Abruption: continuous pain, tender or 'woody' uterus, loss may be concealed.
No digital VE until ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia.
Resuscitate the mother first; transfer from community settings to an obstetric unit.
Anti-D for every non-sensitised RhD-negative woman after APH, with a Kleihauer test after 20 weeks.

summary: You can now define APH and its severity, tell placenta praevia from abruption at the bedside, and explain why digital examination is avoided. You can also give first-line actions, decide on transfer and admission, and apply anti-D and steroid advice under RCOG GTG 63.

A.q: From what gestation does RCOG GTG 63 define vaginal bleeding as an antepartum haemorrhage?
A.why: GTG 63 defines APH as bleeding from or into the genital tract occurring from 24+0 weeks of pregnancy and before the birth of the baby.

whyNot.0: 20+0 weeks is used in anti-D timing, not in the APH definition.
whyNot.1: 22+0 weeks is not the GTG 63 threshold.
whyNot.3: 28+0 weeks is later than the GTG 63 definition.

A.q: A woman at 34 weeks has continuous abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. Her uterus feels hard and tender. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A.why: Continuous pain with a tense, 'woody', tender uterus indicates a significant placental abruption (GTG 63 sections 7 and 7.1).

whyNot.0: Placenta praevia typically causes painless bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.
whyNot.2: A cervical ectropion causes local bleeding without a tense, tender uterus.
whyNot.3: A show is a small mucoid loss; labour pain is intermittent, not continuous with a woody uterus.

A.q: A woman with a known low-lying placenta at 30 weeks presents with painless bleeding. Which examination should NOT be carried out before an ultrasound scan?
A.why: GTG 63 7.3: if placenta praevia is possible, digital vaginal examination should not be performed until ultrasound has excluded it.

whyNot.0: Abdominal palpation is part of assessment, looking for tenderness, tone and contractions.
whyNot.1: A speculum examination can be useful to assess the cervix and look for a local cause.
whyNot.2: The fetal heart should be auscultated as part of the initial assessment.

B.q: An RhD-negative, non-sensitised woman at 30 weeks has an APH. She received RAADP at 28 weeks. What does GTG 63 advise about anti-D?
options: Give anti-D and do a Kleihauer test
No anti-D, as RAADP covers her
Give anti-D after the birth instead
Give anti-D if the Kleihauer is positive
B.why: GTG 63 section 14: give anti-D to all non-sensitised RhD-negative women after any APH, regardless of RAADP; after 20 weeks, at least 500 IU followed by a test for FMH.

whyNot.1: Anti-D is given after APH independent of whether RAADP has been given.
whyNot.2: Waiting until the birth would leave her unprotected from this sensitising event.
whyNot.3: At least 500 IU is given first; the Kleihauer test then decides whether additional anti-D is needed.

B.q: A woman phones a freestanding midwifery unit at 36 weeks with heavy fresh vaginal bleeding. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Come into the midwifery unit now
Rest at home and call if it worsens
Call 999 for transfer to an obstetric unit
B.why: GTG 63 section 6: women with APH presenting outside hospital maternity units should be assessed, stabilised and transferred to a unit with resuscitation, blood transfusion and emergency operative birth facilities.

whyNot.0: A freestanding MLU has no blood bank or theatre, so she would need a second transfer.
whyNot.1: Heavy bleeding needs urgent hospital assessment, not watchful waiting.
whyNot.3: A GP surgery cannot provide the obstetric emergency care she may need.

B.q: A woman at 33 weeks had a major APH that has now stopped. She is stable and the CTG is normal. What should the midwife expect to be offered?
B.why: GTG 63 section 10: offer a single course of antenatal corticosteroids to women between 24+0 and 34+6 weeks who are at risk of preterm birth after APH.

whyNot.0: Going home after a reassuring check is GTG 63 advice for settled spotting; after a major APH she stays in hospital for observation, since the rule is 'at least until the bleeding has stopped'.
whyNot.2: A stable woman with a normal CTG at 33 weeks does not need immediate birth.
whyNot.3: Tocolysis is not routinely used after APH and is not the expected first step here.

C.q: At 35 weeks, Rosa's fresh bleeding began the moment her waters broke. She has no pain and her uterus is soft, but the fetal heart rate quickly becomes abnormal. Which cause should the midwife urgently consider?
C.why: GTG 63 section 7: if APH is associated with rupture of the membranes, bleeding from a ruptured vasa praevia should be considered. The blood is fetal, so the baby is rapidly compromised.

whyNot.1: An ectropion bleeds locally and does not explain sudden fetal compromise at membrane rupture.
whyNot.2: Abruption typically causes continuous pain and a tender uterus; Rosa has neither, and the bleeding began with membrane rupture.
whyNot.3: A show would not cause rapid fetal compromise.

C.q: Aisha, 37 weeks, arrives pale and confused with heavy bleeding; pulse 132, BP 82/46. Fetal heart is not yet heard. What is the priority?
options: Doppler search for the fetal heart
C.why: GTG 63 section 7: with major or massive haemorrhage or a compromised woman, resuscitation starts immediately; the mother is the priority and is stabilised before establishing the fetal condition.

whyNot.0: Scanning delays life-saving resuscitation in a shocked woman.
whyNot.1: Fetal assessment follows once the mother is stable or resuscitation has begun.
whyNot.2: GTG 63 places CTG after maternal stabilisation, not before it.

C.q: A woman at 34 weeks with painful bleeding is scanned and no retroplacental clot is seen. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Abruption is excluded by the scan
The Kleihauer test will confirm it
C.why: GTG 63: abruption is a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound fails to detect about three-quarters of cases, so a normal scan does not exclude it.

whyNot.0: Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption (about 24%), so a clear scan does not exclude it.
whyNot.2: The scan described looked for clot, not placental position; painful bleeding points away from praevia.
whyNot.3: GTG 63 states the Kleihauer test is not a sensitive test for diagnosing abruption.

reteach.title: Ask two questions: does it hurt, and where is the placenta?
reteach.question: If you could ask a bleeding woman only two things, which two would sort praevia from abruption fastest?

blocks.body: Pain that does not go away, with a hard, tender uterus, suggests the placenta is peeling off early (abruption), and some of the blood may be trapped inside. No pain, with a soft uterus and a placenta known to be low, suggests placenta praevia; here a finger in the cervix could start torrential bleeding. Either way, check her pulse and BP first: they tell you how much she has really lost.

blocks.text: Intermittent pain with bleeding suggests labour; continuous pain suggests abruption (GTG 63 section 7).

explain.body: Spotting is staining on the pad; minor is under 50 mL and settled; major is 50 to 1000 mL with no shock; massive is over 1000 mL and/or shock (GTG 63). Visible loss can underestimate concealed bleeding.

test.q: A woman has lost an estimated 300 mL of blood at 35 weeks with normal pulse and BP. How does GTG 63 classify this?
test.why: Major haemorrhage is 50 to 1000 mL with no signs of clinical shock (GTG 63).

whyNot.0: Spotting is staining or streaking, not 300 mL.
whyNot.1: Minor is less than 50 mL that has settled.
whyNot.3: Massive is over 1000 mL and/or signs of shock.

explain.body: Praevia: risk factors include previous praevia, previous caesarean, multiple pregnancy, smoking and assisted conception; bleeding is often painless. Abruption: previous abruption is the strongest predictor; others include pre-eclampsia, FGR, abdominal trauma (including domestic abuse), smoking and cocaine use.

left.label: Praevia
items: Previous caesarean
Previous praevia
Multiple pregnancy

right.label: Abruption
items: Previous abruption
Pre-eclampsia
Abdominal trauma

both.label: Both
items: Smoking
Multiparity
Older age
Assisted conception

test.q: Which history is the strongest predictor of placental abruption?
test.why: GTG 63 section 4.1: the most predictive risk factor for abruption is abruption in a previous pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Previous caesarean is a risk factor for placenta praevia.
whyNot.2: A low-lying placenta suggests placenta praevia, not abruption.
whyNot.3: Assisted conception is listed for both, but it is not the strongest predictor of abruption.

explain.body: Record pulse and BP for every woman with APH. Palpate the abdomen. Avoid digital vaginal examination until ultrasound has excluded praevia; a speculum examination may help. Assess the fetal heart, usually by CTG, once the mother is stable (GTG 63 sections 7-8).

test.q: A woman with painless APH at 31 weeks has not had a scan since 20 weeks. The doctor wants to check her cervix. Which examination is appropriate before an ultrasound?
test.why: A speculum examination can identify cervical dilatation or a local cause; digital examination must wait until ultrasound excludes placenta praevia (GTG 63 7.2-7.3).

whyNot.0: Painless bleeding raises the possibility of praevia, so digital VE must wait for ultrasound.
whyNot.1: A bimanual examination is also digital and could provoke bleeding from a praevia.
whyNot.3: A sweep is digital, is not an assessment tool and could provoke heavy bleeding.

explain.body: Anti-D for every non-sensitised RhD-negative woman after any APH, regardless of RAADP; after 20+0 weeks at least 500 IU then a test for FMH, repeated at least 6-weekly if bleeding recurs. Bleeding heavier than spotting, or ongoing: stay in hospital at least until it stops (GTG 63 sections 9 and 14).

test.q: A woman had spotting at 33 weeks that has stopped; praevia is excluded and checks of her and the baby are reassuring. What is appropriate?
test.why: GTG 63 section 9: women with spotting who are no longer bleeding, with praevia excluded, can go home after a reassuring assessment, with advice to return if bleeding, pain or reduced movements occur.

whyNot.0: Admission until birth is not indicated for settled spotting with praevia excluded.
whyNot.2: Induction is not indicated for settled spotting with reassuring checks.
whyNot.3: There is no evidence base for routine prolonged CTG admission in this situation.
